tips.title: Every kite crosses its sticks at 90°
tips.body: Picture a toy kite: two sticks tied at right angles. Every shape in the kite family has diagonals like that: the **kite** itself, the **rhombus** (a kite with all four sides equal) and the **square**. It only works one way: other quadrilaterals can have diagonals at 90° too, so a right-angle crossing alone does not make a kite.

tips.title: The square inherits everything
tips.body: Draw the family as a tree with the **square at the bottom**. It is a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram and a kite at once, so it has **every** property any of them has. Moving up the tree, each shape loses a property: the rectangle loses equal sides, the rhombus loses right angles.

tips.title: Arrows mean parallel, dashes mean equal
tips.body: Matching **arrows** on two sides mean they are parallel. Matching **dashes** (ticks) mean equal length, and a double dash pairs with a double dash. A small **square** in a corner means 90°. Read these marks first, because they tell you which shape the question is about.

tips.title: Fold it and turn it in your head
tips.body: A **line of symmetry** passes the fold test: every corner lands on a corner. Fold a rectangle along a diagonal and the corners miss, so a diagonal is not a mirror line. For **rotation**, count how many times the shape fits onto itself in one full turn. No rotation symmetry is order **1**, never 0.

tips.title: One angle gives all four
tips.body: In any parallelogram, including a rhombus, **neighbouring angles add to 180°** and **opposite angles are equal**. So one angle of 64° gives the whole set straight away, going round: 64°, 116°, 64°, 116°.

why.matters:
A shape's name is a short way of stating its properties. Call a frame a rectangle and you have said that its corners are right angles, that its opposite sides match and that its diagonals are equal. Call a linkage a rhombus and you have said that its diagonals cross at right angles, however far it is pushed. That is why the definitions have to be exact: each name promises certain properties.

The properties are also tools. Builders use them to check that a frame is square. Engineers use them to make mechanisms that change shape in a controlled way. In an exam you use them to find angles, to decide what a shape must be, and to show that a claim is false with a single counterexample.

examples.title: The scissor lift
examples.body:
The arms of a scissor lift form a column of diamonds, and each diamond is a **rhombus**. Its four sides are the half-arms, which here are **1 m** each, and they stay that length as the lift moves.

The diagonals of a rhombus **bisect each other at right angles**. So half of each diagonal and one side make a right-angled triangle. When the diamond is **1.6 m** across, half of that is 0.8 m, and Pythagoras gives half the height as $\sqrt{1^2 - 0.8^2} = 0.6$ m. The diamond is **1.2 m** tall.

Squeeze it to **1.2 m** across and it becomes **1.6 m** tall. A lift with four sets of arms rises from 4.8 m to 6.4 m. The whole mechanism is a property of the rhombus: the sides stay fixed, and the diagonals trade width for height.

visual.alt: Two diamonds from a scissor lift, each a rhombus with sides of 1 metre and its diagonals drawn in orange: a wide one, 1.6 metres across and 1.2 metres tall, and a narrow one, 1.2 metres across and 1.6 metres tall

examples.title: Checking a gate is square
examples.body:
A gate frame is **2.4 m** by **1.0 m**. As a rectangle, its diagonals are equal: each is **2.6 m**.

Push the top across and the same four bars make a **parallelogram**. The sides have not changed, but the diagonals have. With the top pushed 0.6 m sideways, which drops it to 0.8 m high, they measure about **3.1 m** and **2.0 m**.

That gives two practical facts. A builder checks that a frame is rectangular by measuring **both diagonals**: if the opposite sides match and the diagonals are equal, the corners are right angles. And a diagonal **brace** of 2.6 m stops the sagging, because it turns the frame into triangles, and a triangle with sides 2.4 m, 1.0 m and 2.6 m can only be one shape.

visual.alt: A rectangular gate frame 2.4 metres by 1 metre on a grid of 40 centimetre squares, and dashed over it the same four bars pushed over into a parallelogram that leans to the right

examples.title: The toy kite
examples.body:
A toy kite has a **90 cm** spine and a **60 cm** cross spar, tied at right angles. The spar crosses the spine **25 cm** from the top, at the spar's own midpoint.

The covering then has two short edges of $\sqrt{25^2 + 30^2} \approx 39.1$ cm at the top and two long edges of $\sqrt{65^2 + 30^2} \approx 71.6$ cm at the bottom. That is **two pairs of equal sides next to each other**, the definition of a kite. The diagonals cross at right angles, the spar is cut in half by the spine but not the other way round, and the spine is the **only** line of symmetry.

Move the spar down to the middle of the spine and all four edges become $\sqrt{45^2 + 30^2} \approx 54.1$ cm. The kite has become a **rhombus**, which is the special kind of kite with four equal sides.

visual.alt: A toy kite with a 90 centimetre vertical spine and a 60 centimetre cross spar, both drawn in orange, crossing at right angles 25 centimetres below the top

steps.title: The words and marks every shape question uses
steps.body:
Shape questions are written in a small, exact vocabulary. Learn it first, because the question is often decided by one word.

- A **vertex** is a corner (plural **vertices**). Shapes are named by their vertices **in order round the edge**, so $ABCD$ has sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$.
- A **diagonal** joins two vertices that are not next to each other. In $ABCD$ the diagonals are $AC$ and $BD$.
- **Adjacent** means next to each other; **opposite** means across the shape.
- **Parallel** lines run in the same direction and never meet. They are marked with matching **arrows**.
- **Perpendicular** lines meet at a right angle, marked with a small **square**.
- Sides of **equal length** are marked with matching **dashes**.
- To **bisect** something is to cut it into two equal halves. Two diagonals *bisect each other* when they cross at the midpoint of both.

In the parallelogram $ABCD$ below, the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ cross at $M$. $M$ is the midpoint of both, so they bisect each other.

**Properties and definitions.** A **definition** is the least you need to say to pin a shape down. A parallelogram is *a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides*. Everything else, such as equal opposite sides, equal opposite angles and bisecting diagonals, follows from that. Those extra facts are its **properties**.

visuals.alt: Parallelogram ABCD on a grid, with its diagonals AC and BD drawn in orange and crossing at M, the midpoint of both

check.prompt: What does it mean to say that one line bisects another?
check.solution: To **bisect** is to cut into two equal halves. Crossing at a right angle is *perpendicular*, which is a different property: the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other without being perpendicular.

markScheme.description: cuts it into two equal halves

options: It runs parallel to the other line
It crosses the other at a right angle
It cuts the other exactly in half
It is the same length as the other

steps.title: Triangles
steps.body:
Triangles are named by their **sides** or by their **angles**.

**By sides:**

- **Equilateral**: all three sides equal, so all three angles are equal too. As they add to 180°, each is **60°**.
- **Isosceles**: two sides equal. The two angles at the ends of the third side, the **base angles**, are equal.
- **Scalene**: no sides equal and no angles equal.

**By angles:** a **right-angled** triangle has one angle of 90°. An **acute** triangle has every angle less than 90°, and an **obtuse** triangle has one angle greater than 90°. The two ways of naming combine: a right-angled triangle with two equal sides is a *right-angled isosceles* triangle, with angles 90°, 45° and 45°.

**Symmetry.** An equilateral triangle has **3** lines of symmetry and rotation symmetry of **order 3**. An isosceles triangle has **1** line, down the middle from the vertex between the equal sides. A scalene triangle has none.

**The one to use most.** The equal base angles of an isosceles triangle turn up inside almost every quadrilateral question, because a diagonal often cuts a shape into isosceles triangles. If the angle between the equal sides is 40°, the other two share $180 - 40 = 140°$ equally, so each is $70°$.

visuals.alt: On the left an isosceles triangle ABC with the two sides CA and CB marked equal and the base angles at A and B marked equal; on the right an equilateral triangle PQR with all three sides and all three angles marked equal

A table of triangles. Equilateral: all three sides equal and all angles 60 degrees. Isosceles: two sides equal and two angles equal. Scalene: no sides or angles equal. Right-angled: one angle of 90 degrees, with sides that may or may not be equal.

check.prompt: An isosceles triangle has an angle of $40°$ between its two equal sides. Work out the size of each of the other two angles, in degrees.
check.solution: The other two angles are the equal base angles. They share $180 - 40 = 140°$, so each is $140 \div 2 = 70°$.

steps.title: The six special quadrilaterals
steps.body:
A **quadrilateral** has four sides, and its angles add to **360°**. Six have names, and each is defined by its sides and angles.

- **Square**: four equal sides and four right angles.
- **Rectangle**: four right angles. Its opposite sides are equal.
- **Rhombus**: four equal sides. Its opposite sides are parallel and its opposite angles are equal, but its angles need not be right angles.
- **Parallelogram**: two pairs of parallel sides. Its opposite sides are equal and its opposite angles are equal.
- **Kite**: two pairs of equal sides, each pair **next to each other**. One pair of opposite angles is equal: the pair between the unequal sides. Unless it is also a rhombus, it has no parallel sides.
- **Trapezium**: exactly one pair of parallel sides. If its two non-parallel sides are equal it is an **isosceles trapezium**.

One more property ties the parallelogram family together. **Neighbouring angles in a parallelogram add to 180°**, because they are co-interior angles between a pair of parallel sides. That holds for the rectangle, the rhombus and the square too.

This lesson uses *exactly one pair of parallel sides* for a trapezium. Some books say *at least one pair*, which would make every parallelogram a trapezium as well.

visuals.alt: The six special quadrilaterals drawn on a grid: a square and a rectangle at the top, a parallelogram and a rhombus in the middle, and a kite and a trapezium at the bottom

A table of the six special quadrilaterals. Square: all four sides equal and 2 pairs of parallel sides. Rectangle: opposite sides equal, 2 pairs parallel. Rhombus: all four sides equal, 2 pairs parallel. Parallelogram: opposite sides equal, 2 pairs parallel. Kite: two pairs of equal sides next to each other, no parallel sides. Trapezium: 1 pair of parallel sides and no equal sides needed.

check.prompt: A quadrilateral has four equal sides and two pairs of parallel sides, but none of its angles is a right angle. What is it?
check.solution: Four equal sides with no right angle is a **rhombus**. A square also has four equal sides, but its angles are all right angles.

steps.title: What the diagonals do
steps.body:
Every quadrilateral has two diagonals, and there are three questions to ask about them.

1. **Are they equal in length?**
2. **Do they bisect each other**, crossing at the midpoint of both?
3. **Do they cross at right angles?**

The answers are some of the most useful properties in the topic.

- In every **parallelogram** the diagonals **bisect each other**. That includes the rectangle, the rhombus and the square.
- In a **rectangle** they are also **equal**, but they do not cross at right angles unless it is a square.
- In a **rhombus** they cross at **right angles**, but they are not equal unless it is a square.
- The **square** has all three.
- In a **kite** they cross at right angles, and the diagonal joining the two vertices *between* the equal sides cuts the other in half. It is not cut in half itself.
- A general **trapezium** has none of the three. An isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals, and nothing more.

**A bonus in the rhombus and the square.** Each diagonal also **bisects the angles** at its ends. In a kite, only the main diagonal (the line of symmetry) does that.

visuals.alt: Three quadrilaterals with their diagonals drawn in orange: a rectangle, whose diagonals are equal but do not meet at right angles; a rhombus, whose diagonals cross at right angles at their midpoints; and a kite, whose diagonals cross at right angles with only one of them cut in half

props.title: What the diagonals always do: yes means true of every one

visuals.alt: A table of what is true of the diagonals of every one of the six special quadrilaterals, so no means not always. Square: equal, bisect each other, at right angles. Rectangle: equal and bisect each other, not at right angles. Rhombus: bisect each other at right angles, not equal. Parallelogram: bisect each other only. Kite: at right angles, and one bisects the other. Trapezium: none of the three.

check.prompt: Which of these describes the diagonals of every kite?
check.solution: A kite's diagonals **meet at 90°, and one cuts the other in half**. The main diagonal, which is the line of symmetry, bisects the other one; it is not bisected itself, and the two are not in general equal.
options: They bisect each other, but not at right angles
They are equal in length, and they bisect each other
They meet at 90°, and one cuts the other in half
They are equal in length, and they cross at 90°

steps.title: Symmetry
steps.body:
Two kinds of symmetry, and two numbers to find.

**Line symmetry.** A line of symmetry is a mirror line: fold along it and the two halves match exactly. The quick test is that **every corner must land on a corner**.

**Rotation symmetry.** Turn the shape about its centre. The **order** of rotation symmetry is the number of positions in one full turn where it looks exactly the same. Every shape fits itself at least once, at the end of the full turn, so the smallest possible order is **1**, meaning no rotation symmetry.

**The rectangle and the rhombus swap.** Both have 2 lines of symmetry and order 2, but the lines are in different places.

- A **rectangle's** mirror lines go through the **midpoints of opposite sides**. Its diagonals are **not** mirror lines: fold along one and the corners miss.
- A **rhombus's** mirror lines **are its diagonals**. The lines through the midpoints of its sides are not.

The **parallelogram** is the odd one out: **no** lines of symmetry, but order 2, because a half turn about the crossing of the diagonals maps it onto itself.

**Other plane figures.** A **regular polygon**, with all sides and all angles equal, has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides, and the same order of rotation. A regular hexagon has 6 lines and order 6.

visuals.alt: A rectangle with its two lines of symmetry drawn in green, running through the midpoints of opposite sides, beside a rhombus whose two lines of symmetry, also in green, are its diagonals

props.title: Lines of symmetry and order of rotation

visuals.alt: A table of symmetry. Square: 4 lines, order 4. Rectangle: 2 lines, order 2. Rhombus: 2 lines, order 2. Parallelogram: no lines, order 2. Kite: 1 line, order 1. Trapezium: no lines, order 1. Isosceles trapezium: 1 line, order 1.

check.prompt: A rectangle is not a square. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
check.solution: **2**: one through the midpoints of each pair of opposite sides. The diagonals are not lines of symmetry, because folding along one does not make the corners meet.

steps.title: The family: every square is a rhombus
steps.body:
The special quadrilaterals are not separate boxes. Some are special cases of others, and a shape keeps every property of the families it belongs to.

- A **square** has four right angles, so it **is a rectangle**. It has four equal sides, so it **is a rhombus**.
- A **rectangle** and a **rhombus** each have two pairs of parallel sides, so each **is a parallelogram**.
- A **rhombus** has two pairs of equal sides next to each other, so it **is a kite** too.

The arrows only go one way. **Every square is a rectangle**, but a rectangle is a square only when its sides are all equal.

**Why it matters.** It decides questions such as *"which shapes have diagonals that bisect each other?"* The answer is the parallelogram **and everything inside its family**: the rectangle, the rhombus and the square.

**Being two things at once.** A shape that is both a rhombus and a rectangle has four equal sides **and** four right angles, so it is a square.

props.title: Every one of these is also a special case of the next

visuals.alt: A table of the family of quadrilaterals: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus; every rectangle is a parallelogram; every rhombus is a parallelogram and a kite

check.prompt: A quadrilateral is a rhombus and a rectangle at the same time. What can you say about it?
check.solution: A rhombus has four equal sides and a rectangle has four right angles. Both at once means **it must be a square**.

steps.title: Worked examples: using properties to find angles
steps.body: Angle questions on quadrilaterals nearly always need one property of the shape and one angle fact. The skill is choosing the property. Name it in your working, because the reason is part of the answer.

visuals.problem: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. Angle $BAD = 110°$ and angle $BCD = 50°$. Work out angle $ABC$.

steps.text: In a kite, the pair of **opposite angles between the unequal sides** are equal. Here those are the angles at $B$ and $D$.
steps.note: The kite is symmetrical about $AC$, which carries $B$ onto $D$.

steps.text: The angles of a quadrilateral add to $360°$, so angles $B$ and $D$ together make $360 - 110 - 50 = 200°$.

visuals.problem: In parallelogram $PQRS$, angle $P = (3x + 10)°$ and angle $Q = (2x + 20)°$. Work out $x$, and then all four angles.

steps.text: $P$ and $Q$ are **neighbouring** angles of a parallelogram, so they add to $180°$.
steps.note: They are co-interior angles between the parallel sides $PS$ and $QR$.

steps.text: Opposite angles are equal, so $R = 100°$ and $S = 80°$.

visuals.alt: Kite ABCD with AB equal to AD and CB equal to CD, drawn with its line of symmetry AC in green; the angle at A is 110 degrees and the angle at C is 50 degrees, and the angles at B and D are equal

check.prompt: $PQRS$ is a rhombus. Angle $PQR = 70°$. The diagonal $PR$ is drawn. Work out angle $QPR$, in degrees.
check.solution: $PQ = QR$ because all the sides of a rhombus are equal, so triangle $PQR$ is **isosceles** and its base angles $QPR$ and $QRP$ are equal. They share $180 - 70 = 110°$, so angle $QPR = 55°$.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**1.** A quadrilateral has diagonals that are equal and bisect each other, but do not cross at right angles. Name it.

**2.** A parallelogram has one angle of 47°. Work out the other three.

**3.** A kite has angles of 90° and 60° at the two ends of its line of symmetry. Work out each of the other two angles.

**4.** True or false: (a) every rhombus is a parallelogram; (b) every parallelogram is a rhombus.

**Answers.** 1. A **rectangle**. A square's diagonals would cross at right angles. 2. Going round: **133°, 47° and 133°**, because neighbouring angles add to 180° and opposite angles are equal. 3. The other two are equal and share $360 - 90 - 60 = 210°$, so each is **105°**. 4. (a) **True**: a rhombus has two pairs of parallel sides. (b) **False**: a parallelogram need not have four equal sides.

visuals.alt: A table of the answers to the four practice questions: a rectangle; 133, 47 and 133 degrees; 105 degrees each; and true then false

check.prompt: A quadrilateral has rotation symmetry of order 2 and exactly two lines of symmetry, and those lines are its diagonals. What is it?
check.solution: A **rhombus**: its two mirror lines are its diagonals. A rectangle also has two lines and order 2, but its mirror lines go through the midpoints of the sides. A square has four lines, and a trapezium has order 1.

steps.title: Going deeper: proving properties, and breaking false claims
steps.body:
**Proving a property.** The properties are not just facts to learn; each one can be derived. Here is why the diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles.

$ABCD$ is a rhombus, with diagonals meeting at $M$.

1. $AB = AD$, because all sides of a rhombus are equal.
2. $BM = DM$, because a rhombus is a parallelogram, and the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
3. $AM$ is common to both triangles.
4. So triangles $ABM$ and $ADM$ are congruent (**SSS**).
5. So angle $AMB$ = angle $AMD$. They lie on the straight line $BD$, so they add to $180°$, and each is $90°$.

Each line gives a reason, and the proof ends by stating what was to be shown.

**Breaking a false claim.** To show that a claim is false, one **counterexample** is enough. Choose a shape that meets the condition but is not the shape claimed.

- *"Four equal sides makes a square."* A **rhombus that is not a square** has four equal sides and no right angle.
- *"Equal diagonals make a rectangle."* An **isosceles trapezium** has equal diagonals.
- *"Diagonals at right angles make a rhombus."* So do a **kite's**.
- *"Equal diagonals at right angles make a square."* The kite with vertices $(0, 4)$, $(3, 0)$, $(0, -2)$ and $(-3, 0)$ has diagonals of 6 and 6 crossing at right angles, and it is not a square. What is missing is that the diagonals must **also bisect each other**.

**Algebra with a twist.** In rhombus $ABCD$, angle $A = (4x + 10)°$ and angle $C = (2x + 50)°$. Opposite angles are equal, so $4x + 10 = 2x + 50$ and $x = 20$. Then angle $A = 90°$. A rhombus with a right angle has four right angles, so $ABCD$ is a **square**. Once you have an angle, always ask what it tells you about the shape.

props.title: A property, and a shape that has it without being the shape claimed

visuals.alt: A table of four false claims and a counterexample to each: four equal sides does not make a square (a rhombus); equal diagonals do not make a rectangle (an isosceles trapezium); diagonals at right angles do not make a rhombus (a kite); equal diagonals at right angles do not make a square (a kite with both diagonals 6 long)

check.prompt: A student claims that any quadrilateral with equal diagonals is a rectangle. Which shape is a counterexample?
check.solution: **An isosceles trapezium** has equal diagonals but only one pair of parallel sides, so it is not a rectangle. A square is a rectangle, so it cannot break the claim; a rhombus and a general parallelogram do not have equal diagonals.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Vertices** are named in order round the shape; a **diagonal** joins two vertices that are not next to each other.
- **Arrows** mark parallel sides, **dashes** mark equal sides, and a small **square** marks a right angle.
- **Equilateral**: 3 equal sides, all 60°. **Isosceles**: 2 equal sides and equal **base angles**. **Scalene**: none equal.
- A **parallelogram** has two pairs of parallel sides, equal opposite sides and angles, and **neighbouring angles adding to 180°**.
- A **rectangle** adds right angles; a **rhombus** adds four equal sides; a **square** has both.
- A **kite** has two pairs of equal sides next to each other, and one pair of equal opposite angles.
- A **trapezium** has exactly one pair of parallel sides.
- Diagonals **bisect each other** in every parallelogram. They are **equal** in the rectangle and square, and **at right angles** in the rhombus, square and kite.
- A rectangle's mirror lines join the midpoints of its sides; a rhombus's mirror lines are its diagonals. A parallelogram has **no** lines but **order 2**.
- Every square is a rectangle and a rhombus. Every rectangle and rhombus is a parallelogram, and every rhombus is a kite.
- A claim is broken by **one counterexample**.

visuals.alt: The six special quadrilaterals drawn on a grid: a square and a rectangle at the top, a parallelogram and a rhombus in the middle, and a kite and a trapezium at the bottom

check.prompt: Which quadrilateral has no lines of symmetry but rotation symmetry of order 2?
check.solution: A **parallelogram** that is not a rectangle or a rhombus. A half turn about the point where its diagonals cross maps it onto itself, but no fold does. A rectangle has two lines of symmetry, a kite has one, and a general trapezium has order 1.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it?
questions.solution: Exactly one pair of parallel sides is the definition of a **trapezium**. A rhombus, a parallelogram and a rectangle all have two pairs.

questions.prompt: A rhombus is not a square. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
questions.solution: **2**: its two diagonals. The lines through the midpoints of opposite sides are mirror lines for a rectangle, not for a rhombus.

questions.prompt: Which type of triangle has exactly one line of symmetry?
questions.solution: An **isosceles triangle** (that is not equilateral) has one line of symmetry, from the vertex between the equal sides to the midpoint of the opposite side. An equilateral triangle has three, a scalene triangle has none, and a right-angled triangle has one only when it is also isosceles.

questions.prompt: An isosceles triangle has two equal base angles of $72°$. Work out the size of the third angle, in degrees.
questions.solution: The two base angles total $2 \times 72 = 144°$. The angles of a triangle add to $180°$, so the third angle is $180 - 144 = 36°$.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has four right angles. Its diagonals are equal, but they do not cross at right angles. Give the most precise name for the quadrilateral.
questions.solution: A **rectangle**. It cannot be a square, because a square's diagonals cross at right angles.

questions.prompt: Which list contains every special quadrilateral whose diagonals always cross at right angles?
questions.solution: The diagonals cross at right angles in the **square, rhombus and kite**, the kite family. A rectangle's diagonals are equal but not perpendicular, and a parallelogram's only bisect each other.

questions.prompt: A parallelogram is not a rectangle or a rhombus. What is its order of rotation symmetry?
questions.solution: **2**: a half turn about the point where the diagonals cross maps it onto itself, and a quarter turn does not. Order 1 would mean no rotation symmetry, and an order of 0 is never possible.

questions.prompt: One angle of a parallelogram is $64°$. Work out the size of an angle next to it, in degrees.
questions.solution: Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add to $180°$ (co-interior angles between parallel sides), so the angle is $180 - 64 = 116°$.

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. Angle $BAD = 80°$ and angle $BCD = 60°$. Work out angle $ABC$, in degrees.
questions.solution: In a kite the angles between the unequal sides are equal: here angles $B$ and $D$. The angles of a quadrilateral add to $360°$, so $B$ and $D$ share $360 - 80 - 60 = 220°$, and angle $ABC = 220 \div 2 = 110°$.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements is always true?
questions.solution: **Every square is a rectangle**: it has four right angles, which is all a rectangle needs. The others fail: a rectangle need not have equal sides, and a rhombus or a parallelogram need not have right angles.

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is a rhombus with angle $BAD = 130°$. The diagonal $BD$ is drawn. Work out angle $ABD$, in degrees.
questions.solution: $AB = AD$, since all the sides of a rhombus are equal, so triangle $ABD$ is isosceles with equal base angles $ABD$ and $ADB$. They share $180 - 130 = 50°$, so angle $ABD = 25°$.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has four equal sides, and none of its angles is a right angle. Give the most precise name for the quadrilateral.
questions.solution: A **rhombus**: four equal sides, and angles that need not be right angles. With right angles it would be a square.

questions.prompt: Sam says: "A quadrilateral with four equal sides must be a square." Which reply is correct?
questions.solution: **Wrong: a rhombus need not have any right angles.** A rhombus that is not a square has four equal sides and no right angle, and one counterexample is enough. A square needs four right angles as well, and a rhombus is not a tilted square, because tilting does not change its angles.
options: Right: four equal sides is all a square needs
Wrong: a rhombus need not have any right angles
Wrong: a trapezium can also have four equal sides
Right: a rhombus is only a square turned on its corner

questions.prompt: Priya says: "A rectangle has four lines of symmetry: two through the midpoints of opposite sides, and its two diagonals." Is she right?
questions.solution: **No: fold along a diagonal and the corners do not meet**, so a rectangle has only the two lines through the midpoints of opposite sides. Its diagonals are equal, but being equal does not make them mirror lines. Only in a square are the diagonals mirror lines too.

markScheme.description: no; diagonals are not mirror lines

options: No: fold along a diagonal and the corners do not meet
Yes: every diagonal of a quadrilateral is a mirror line

questions.prompt: $PQRS$ is a parallelogram. Angle $P = (5x - 20)°$ and the opposite angle $R = (3x + 30)°$. Work out the size of angle $Q$, in degrees.
questions.solution: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: $5x - 20 = 3x + 30$, so $2x = 50$ and $x = 25$. Then angle $P = 5 \times 25 - 20 = 105°$. $Q$ is next to $P$, so angle $Q = 180 - 105 = 75°$.

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is a kite with $AB = AD$ and $CB = CD$. Angle $ABC = (2x + 15)°$, angle $ADC = (3x - 10)°$ and angle $BAD = 4x°$. Work out the size of angle $BCD$, in degrees.
questions.solution: The angles at $B$ and $D$ lie between the unequal sides, so they are equal: $2x + 15 = 3x - 10$, giving $x = 25$. So $B = D = 65°$ and angle $BAD = 4 \times 25 = 100°$. The angles add to $360°$: angle $BCD = 360 - 65 - 65 - 100 = 130°$.

markScheme.description: x = 25, and 360 minus the other three angles

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is a rhombus, and its diagonals cross at $M$. Angle $MAB = 28°$. Work out the size of angle $ABC$, in degrees.
questions.solution: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles, so angle $AMB = 90°$. In triangle $ABM$, angle $ABM = 180 - 90 - 28 = 62°$. The diagonal $BD$ bisects angle $ABC$, so angle $ABC = 2 \times 62 = 124°$.

markScheme.description: 124, doubling because BD bisects the angle

visual.alt: Rhombus ABCD with its diagonals AC and BD drawn in orange, crossing at M

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is a rhombus whose diagonals meet at $M$. A proof uses only these three facts: $AB = AD$, $BM = DM$, and $AM$ is common to triangles $ABM$ and $ADM$. Which condition shows that the two triangles are congruent?
questions.solution: **SSS**: the three facts are three pairs of equal sides. No angle is used, so SAS and ASA do not apply, and RHS needs a right angle that has not yet been shown.

questions.prompt: A quadrilateral has diagonals that are equal in length and cross at right angles. A student says it must be a square. Is the student right?
questions.solution: **No: a kite can have equal diagonals at right angles.** The kite with vertices $(0, 4)$, $(3, 0)$, $(0, -2)$ and $(-3, 0)$ has diagonals of length 6 and 6 that cross at right angles. It is not a square, because its diagonals do not bisect each other. A rectangle that is not a square does not have perpendicular diagonals.

markScheme.description: no, a kite is a counterexample

No: a rectangle has equal diagonals at 90° too

questions.prompt: Prove that the diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles. You may use the fact that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
questions.solution:
Let $ABCD$ be a rhombus whose diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ cross at $M$.

$AB = AD$, because all four sides of a rhombus are equal.

A rhombus is a parallelogram, and the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $BM = DM$.

$AM$ is a side of both triangle $ABM$ and triangle $ADM$.

So triangles $ABM$ and $ADM$ are congruent (SSS), and their corresponding angles are equal: angle $AMB$ = angle $AMD$.

Angles $AMB$ and $AMD$ lie on the straight line $BD$, so they add to $180°$. Two equal angles adding to $180°$ are each $90°$.

So the diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles.

questions.prompt: The points $A(1, 1)$, $B(5, 2)$, $C(6, 6)$ and $D(2, 5)$ are joined in order. Show that $ABCD$ is a rhombus, and decide, with a reason, whether it is a square.
questions.solution:
**Sides.** From $A$ to $B$ is 4 across and 1 up, so $AB = \sqrt{4^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{17}$. From $B$ to $C$ is 1 across and 4 up, so $BC = \sqrt{17}$. From $C$ to $D$ is 4 back and 1 down, and from $D$ to $A$ is 1 back and 4 down, so $CD = DA = \sqrt{17}$.

All four sides are equal, so $ABCD$ is a **rhombus**.

**Square?** A square's diagonals are equal. $AC$ runs 5 across and 5 up, so $AC = \sqrt{50}$. $BD$ runs 3 back and 3 up, so $BD = \sqrt{18}$. The diagonals are **not equal**, so $ABCD$ is **not a square**.

(Equally: the step $AB$ has gradient $\tfrac{1}{4}$ and the step $BC$ has gradient $4$. Their product is $1$, not $-1$, so angle $ABC$ is not a right angle.)

questions.prompt: $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezium. $AB$ is parallel to $DC$ and $AD = BC$. Angle $DAB = (2x + 10)°$ and angle $ADC = (x + 20)°$. Work out the size of angle $ABC$, in degrees.
questions.solution: $DAB$ and $ADC$ are co-interior angles between the parallel sides $AB$ and $DC$, so they add to $180°$: $3x + 30 = 180$, so $x = 50$ and angle $DAB = 110°$. In an isosceles trapezium the two angles on the same parallel side are equal, so angle $ABC$ = angle $DAB = 110°$.

markScheme.description: angle ABC = 110, by the symmetry of the isosceles trapezium

examTechnique.body:
Name the property you use, in words, every time. "Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal" or "the diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles" is the reason, and a reason is part of what an angle question asks for.

Read the marks on the diagram before anything else. Arrows, dashes and right-angle squares tell you which sides are parallel, which are equal and where the right angles are. The name of the shape tells you the rest.

For a kite, find the line of symmetry first. The equal angles are the pair it carries onto each other, the ones between the unequal sides, and not the pair it passes through.

When a question gives angles in terms of $x$, write the equation from a property: equal opposite angles, neighbouring angles adding to $180°$, or all four adding to $360°$. Solve it, substitute back, and check that the angles add to $360°$.

To show that a claim about shapes is false, give one counterexample and say which part of the claim it breaks. To prove a property, use congruent triangles, and give a reason for every equal side or angle.
examinerErrors: Giving an angle with no reason, or a reason that names the wrong property.
Taking the equal angles of a kite to be the pair on its line of symmetry, rather than the pair between the unequal sides.
Counting the diagonals of a rectangle as lines of symmetry.
Giving the order of rotation symmetry as 0 for a shape with none, instead of 1.
Treating a rhombus as a square turned on its corner, and so giving it right angles.
Forgetting that a square is also a rectangle and a rhombus when asked which shapes have a property.
Solving for x and stopping there, when the question asks for an angle.
Using a shape that is itself an example of the claim when a counterexample is asked for, such as a square to break a claim about rectangles.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the definitions as exact. It knows that a square is a rectangle and a rhombus, that a rhombus is a parallelogram and a kite, and it uses those links to answer "which shapes" questions completely. It finds angles by naming one property and one angle fact at each step, and it notices when an answer changes what the shape is: a rhombus with a right angle is a square. When a claim is false it gives a single, precise counterexample. When a property must be proved it builds congruent triangles, gives a reason for each equal side or angle, and finishes by stating the result it was asked to prove.
